passage: Nikita had rehearsed the sentence on the metro all the way to campus. Professor Tanuja's door was half open, and the deadline for the exchange programme was still five weeks away, which felt safe. She knocked. "Ma'am, may I ask for a recommendation letter? I know it's a favour." She held out a folder: her résumé, the two lab reports from Professor Tanuja's course, and a short paragraph on why she wanted the programme. "I put the deadline on the first page." Tanuja flipped through it and nodded. "This makes it easy. Come back in two weeks and remind me." Nikita's shoulders dropped. She had almost told herself that professors write these letters automatically, and she was glad she hadn't.

qa.q: How many weeks were left before the exchange programme deadline?
What was Nikita feeling as she knocked, and what shows it?
qa.a: She was nervous: she rehearsed the sentence on the metro and called the request a favour, and her shoulders dropping afterwards shows relief.

qa.q: What made Nikita's request easy to say yes to?
qa.a: She asked early and politely and gave context: a résumé, two lab reports, a paragraph on her aims and the deadline. 🙂

qa.q: How might Professor Tanuja see the folder?
qa.a: Professor Tanuja probably sees that it saves effort and shows Nikita is serious, which fits the remark "This makes it easy."

grounding: A student worried about asking asks early and politely and gives context about her work.

passage:
Anders had drafted the email to Professor Hana Berg six times. The master's application in Copenhagen was due in five weeks, and he needed a letter. He had taken two of her courses and worked on one research project, but she taught two hundred students a year. What if she didn't remember him?
His roommate suggested just writing, "Please write me a letter by Friday." Anders winced.
Instead he wrote: "Dear Professor Berg, I'm applying to the Environmental Science master's in Copenhagen, due 15 March. I took your Soil Ecology course and worked on the wetland sampling project with your group last spring. Would you feel able to write a recommendation? I've attached my CV, a short summary of my project work and my draft statement. If it isn't possible, I completely understand."
He sent it at 9 a.m. on a Tuesday. By lunch she had replied: "Of course I remember the wetland data; your field notes were the tidiest in the group. Happy to write. Thank you for giving me time."

qa.q: When was the Copenhagen application due?
What worried Anders about asking Professor Berg?
qa.a: He feared she wouldn't remember him among two hundred students a year, which made him anxious about asking.

qa.q: What made Anders's request a good one?
qa.a: He asked five weeks early and politely, reminded her of his course and project, attached his CV, summary and statement, and made it easy for her to say no.

qa.q: How did Professor Berg feel about the request?
qa.a: Pleased; she remembered his tidy field notes and thanked him for giving her time.

grounding: Shows worrying about asking for a recommendation, and asking early and politely with context about one's work.

passage:
In the department office, Harsha stood behind three other students waiting for Dr. Vinita Pai, his stomach tight. Two days earlier he had listed her as a referee on a scholarship form without asking, assuming she wouldn't mind. The scholarship office had emailed her directly. She hadn't replied to his messages since.
When his turn came, he didn't make excuses. "Ma'am, I'm sorry. I put your name on the state merit scholarship form without asking. That was wrong. If you're not comfortable, I'll withdraw your name today."
Dr. Pai looked at him for a while. "Yes, it was wrong. I don't write for people who haven't asked me." Then, more gently: "What do you need it for, and what have you done in my class that I should know about?"
He showed her his term project, his lab reports, and a one-page note on why he was applying. She read it. "Next time, ask first, and give me two weeks. I'll write this one."

qa.a: In the department office, behind three other students.
He felt anxious and guilty for having listed Dr. Pai as a referee without asking her.

qa.q: How did Harsha repair the mistake?
qa.a: He apologised without excuses, offered to withdraw her name, and gave her his project, lab reports and a note on why he was applying.

qa.q: How does Dr. Pai see what Harsha did?
qa.a: As wrong, since she writes only when asked, but she is willing to help once he owns it and gives context.

grounding: Illustrates the mistake of using a professor's name without asking, and repairing it by asking politely and giving context about one's work.
